lesson.title: Spanning Tree Protocol: Taming Loops Without Losing Redundancy
lesson.summary: Spanning Tree Protocol lets network engineers wire redundant links between switches for reliability, while automatically blocking just enough of those links to leave a loop free logical path for every frame. Without it, a redundant Ethernet topology would melt itself down in a broadcast storm within seconds.
lesson.body:
Physical redundancy is good engineering: if a network has only one cable connecting two switches and that cable fails, the network splits in two. The obvious fix is to run a second cable as a backup. But Ethernet frames were never designed with this kind of redundancy in mind. A frame has no hop count or time to live field the way an IP packet does, so nothing stops a frame from circulating forever if the wiring between bridges or switches happens to form a loop. Combine that with the flooding behavior bridges and switches fall back on for broadcast frames or frames with an unknown destination, and a redundant, looped topology does not just tolerate the extra link, it destroys itself: a single flooded frame gets duplicated at every loop traversal, doubling and redoubling until the resulting broadcast storm consumes all available bandwidth within seconds.

Spanning Tree Protocol, standardized as IEEE 802.1D, solves this by having bridges and switches cooperate to compute a loop free logical topology on top of whatever physical wiring exists, redundant links included. Switches exchange periodic messages called Bridge Protocol Data Units, or BPDUs, which carry enough information for the network to agree on three things. First, they elect a single root bridge, the switch with the lowest bridge identifier, the reference point the tree is built around. Second, every other switch determines its own root port, the port offering the lowest cost path back to the root bridge. Third, for every segment shared by more than one switch, the switches agree on a single designated port, responsible for forwarding traffic onto that segment. Any port that is neither a root port nor a designated port is placed into a blocking state.

Blocking does not mean disconnected. A blocked port still listens for BPDUs, it simply does not forward data frames. This preserves the benefit of the redundant cabling: the backup link is physically present and monitored the entire time, so if the active link or an active switch fails, the blocked port can transition back to forwarding and restore connectivity, without a human touching a cable.

Picture three switches, A, B, and C, wired in a triangle: a link between A and B, a link between B and C, and a redundant link directly between C and A. Suppose switch A has the lowest bridge ID and becomes the root. Switch B's port toward A becomes its root port, its shortest path to the root. Switch C has two paths to the root, directly through the C to A link or indirectly through B; if the direct link has the lower cost, it becomes C's root port. On the B to C segment, both switches have claimed root ports elsewhere, so they compare costs to pick the designated port, typically B's, since B is closer to the root. C's port on that link, having lost, drops into blocking. The loop is now broken at one point, and every frame has exactly one path through the tree.

Classic 802.1D is deliberately cautious: after a topology change, a formerly blocked port passes through listening and learning states before it forwards again, taking up to about fifty seconds in the worst case, since it waits out a maximum age timer plus two forward delay periods. That caution avoids temporary loops during the transition but is slow for modern networks, which is why Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol, standardized later as 802.1w, was introduced to reach a stable, loop free state far faster while keeping the same root bridge and designated port logic. Either way, spanning tree lets designers build in physical redundancy without gambling on a broadcast storm.
